name: Attachment Style Test
tagline: Discover how you bond, trust and seek closeness in relationships.
intro: Your attachment style shapes how you connect with partners, friends and family: how much you worry about being left, and how comfortable you are with closeness. This test measures two dimensions, attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance, and combines them into one of four styles. Answer based on how you generally feel in close relationships. It takes about five minutes.
seoTitle: Attachment Style Test – Free online quiz
seoDescription: Are you secure, anxious, avoidant or fearful? Take this 5-minute attachment style test and get a personal report on how you bond and trust.

anxiety.name: Attachment anxiety
anxiety.short: How much you worry about rejection, abandonment and whether you are loved enough.
anxiety.low: Your answers suggest you feel fairly secure about being loved. You do not need a lot of reassurance, you can let people have their own space and a quiet day or an unanswered message rarely sends you into worry. This inner calm is a real strength in relationships. Keep using it to stay open and generous. One tip: make sure your easy-going attitude does not lead you to overlook a partner who does need more reassurance than you do. Ask them what helps them feel safe.
anxiety.mid: You feel secure much of the time, but some situations can trigger worry about where you stand. Mixed signals, distance after a conflict or a change in plans may set off doubts that take a while to settle. This is very common. Try to notice the moment the worry starts and check the facts before acting on it. It also helps to tell people you trust what reassures you, in a calm moment, so you can ask for it directly instead of searching for clues.
anxiety.high: Your answers suggest that fear of rejection or abandonment plays a big role in your relationships. You may scan for signs that someone is pulling away, need a lot of reassurance or feel your mood rise and fall with the relationship. This pattern usually grows from earlier experiences and can change. Practise soothing yourself first, for example with a walk or a short breathing exercise, before reaching out. Building a life with your own sources of meaning also helps. A therapist can support you in feeling more secure.

avoidance.name: Attachment avoidance
avoidance.short: How uncomfortable you are with emotional closeness and depending on others.
avoidance.low: Your answers suggest you are comfortable with closeness. You can lean on others, share what goes on inside you and let people lean on you in return. This openness makes deep and lasting bonds possible. Keep investing in it. One tip: closeness works best with healthy boundaries, so make sure you also keep some time and interests that are just yours. That way intimacy stays a choice rather than something you depend on for your sense of balance.
avoidance.mid: You value closeness, but you also guard your independence. In some moments, for instance when emotions run high or a relationship becomes more serious, you may pull back or keep certain things to yourself. That is understandable and not a problem in itself. Try to notice when you retreat and ask whether you need space or are avoiding vulnerability. Sharing one small personal thing more than usual, and seeing how it is received, can gradually make openness feel safer.
avoidance.high: Your answers suggest that closeness can feel uncomfortable or even threatening to you. You may prefer to rely on yourself, keep feelings private and need distance when someone gets too near. This often develops as a way of protecting yourself and it can feel like freedom. Yet it may also leave you or your partner feeling lonely. Practise naming one feeling a day to someone you trust, and stay in emotional conversations a little longer than feels natural. A therapist can help you explore this safely.

summary: Attachment is measured on two scales: anxiety (worry about being rejected) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness). Low scores on both point to a secure style; the combination of your two scores determines your overall style. Your result describes tendencies, not fixed traits, and attachment styles can change with new experiences.

secure.name: Secure
secure.text: Your answers suggest a secure attachment style. You generally trust that the people you love care about you, and you feel comfortable both being close and having time apart. You can express your needs, listen to those of others and handle disagreements without fearing the relationship will end. This does not mean your relationships are free of problems, but you tend to approach them with confidence and openness. Keep nurturing this by staying curious about your partner's inner world and by being patient with people who feel less secure than you. Your calm can help them feel safer too.

anxious.name: Anxious-preoccupied
anxious.text: Your answers suggest an anxious-preoccupied style. You value closeness highly and are very attuned to the people you love, but you may also worry about losing them. Delayed replies, distance or conflict can trigger strong feelings and a need for reassurance. Your warmth and loyalty are real strengths. The challenge is to feel safe from the inside rather than depending on constant signs from others. Practise calming yourself before reacting, share your needs clearly instead of testing people, and invest in friendships and activities that support your self-worth. Partners who are consistent and open help this style feel more secure.

avoidant.name: Dismissive-avoidant
avoidant.text: Your answers suggest a dismissive-avoidant style. You value independence and self-reliance and may feel uncomfortable when others want a lot of closeness or depend on you emotionally. You often handle problems alone and keep your feelings private. This can make you calm and capable under pressure, but partners may experience you as distant. The opportunity for growth lies in letting people in a little more. Try sharing small worries, accepting help when it is offered and staying present when conversations become emotional. Closeness does not have to mean losing your freedom; it can become a safe base from which to explore.

fearful.name: Fearful-avoidant
fearful.text: Your answers suggest a fearful-avoidant style. You may long for closeness while also fearing it, so relationships can feel confusing: you move towards people and then pull back when it becomes intense. Worry about rejection and discomfort with depending on others can exist side by side. This style often grows from experiences where closeness did not feel safe, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. Be gentle with yourself and look for steady, predictable relationships. Learning to notice and name your feelings helps a lot. Working with a qualified therapist can be especially valuable for building a more secure way of connecting.
